points.title: Using economic indicators as evidence
points.brief: Figures such as the unemployment rate or inflation give hard evidence for a claim about the economy, but check the period and source they cover.

points.title: Short-term and long-term effects
points.brief: A decision can help now and cost later, or the reverse, such as borrowing for study, so weigh effects over time as well as on different groups.

points.title: Spotting bias in a source
points.brief: A source can lean one way because of who made it or paid for it, so compare it with others and look for data, not only opinion.

points.title: Recommending a course of action
points.brief: A recommendation names the best option, explains why it beats the others on the criteria, and says what it will cost and who it will affect.

points.title: What an economic indicator is
points.brief: An economic indicator is a statistic that shows how the economy is going, such as the growth rate, unemployment or inflation.

points.title: Economic growth and GDP
points.brief: Gross domestic product is the value of all goods and services made in a country in a year. Economic growth is GDP rising.

points.title: The unemployment rate
points.brief: The unemployment rate is the share of people in the labour force who are looking for work but have none.

points.title: Inflation
points.brief: Inflation is a general rise in prices over time, measured in Australia by the consumer price index, so each dollar buys less.

points.title: Material and non-material living standards
points.brief: Material living standards are the goods and services people can buy. Non-material ones include health, safety, free time and a clean environment.

points.title: The government's economic objectives
points.brief: The Australian Government aims for steady economic growth, full employment and stable prices, to keep living standards rising.

points.title: Responding to indicators
points.brief: When indicators change, the government acts, such as funding apprenticeships and training places when unemployment rises.

points.title: Fiscal policy
points.brief: Fiscal policy is the government's use of its spending and taxes to manage the economy, such as spending more to support jobs in a slowdown.

points.title: The federal Budget
points.brief: Each year the federal Budget sets out the government's planned spending and revenue. Spending more than it collects is a deficit, and less is a surplus.

points.title: Income and wealth
points.brief: Income is money received over a period, such as wages. Wealth is the value of what someone owns, such as a home, savings and shares, less what they owe.

points.title: Why living standards differ
points.brief: Unemployment, low pay, illness and where people live mean some Australians have much lower living standards than others, and some live in poverty.

points.title: Progressive taxation
points.brief: A progressive tax takes a larger share of income as income rises, which narrows the gap between high and low incomes.

points.title: Transfer payments
points.brief: Transfer payments are government payments to people who need support, such as the Age Pension, Youth Allowance and JobSeeker Payment.

points.title: Services for everyone
points.brief: Medicare and public schools give everyone health care and education whatever their income, which lifts living standards for people on low incomes.

points.title: Minor and major decisions
points.brief: A minor decision, such as lunch, costs little and is easy to undo. A major one, such as a car or a home, costs a lot, lasts years and needs planning.

points.title: What influences a major purchase
points.brief: Price, finance available, marketing, convenience, age and ethical or environmental concerns all shape what people decide to buy.

points.title: The cost of borrowing
points.brief: A loan costs more than its price because of interest and fees, so check the interest rate, the total repaid and whether you can meet each repayment.

points.title: The full cost of a car
points.brief: A car costs more than its price, with registration, insurance, fuel, servicing and depreciation, the fall in its value over time.

points.title: Buying a home
points.brief: Most people buy a home with a deposit and a mortgage, a loan repaid over many years, which also brings costs such as rates, insurance and repairs.

points.title: What superannuation is
points.brief: Superannuation is money saved during working life, invested and kept until retirement, so people have income when they stop work.

points.title: The superannuation guarantee
points.brief: Employers must pay a set share of each worker's wages into their super fund. Workers can also add their own money.

points.title: Superannuation investment options
points.brief: Funds offer options from safer to riskier. Younger workers often choose growth options because they have decades to recover from falls.

points.title: Managing your superannuation
points.brief: Check fees and returns, combine several accounts into one, and find lost super, so fees do not eat into your savings.

points.title: Superannuation and the Age Pension
points.brief: More super means fewer people need the full Age Pension, which eases the cost to government as the population ages.

points.title: What productivity is
points.brief: Productivity is how much is produced from the resources used, such as output per hour worked. Higher productivity lets wages and living standards rise.

points.title: Ways to raise productivity
points.brief: Businesses raise productivity through training, new equipment and technology, research, and methods such as just-in-time stock that cut waste.

points.title: Organisational structures
points.brief: A vertical structure has many levels of managers. A flat, horizontal structure has few, so decisions are quicker and workers have more say.

points.title: Managing a workforce
points.brief: Businesses keep good workers with fair pay, flexible hours, paid parental leave, safe workplaces and chances to use their initiative.

points.title: First Nations workforce and business programs
points.brief: Programs such as cross-cultural training, Indigenous employment targets and First Nations chambers of commerce help First Nations Australians find work and start businesses.

points.title: Entrepreneurs and change
points.brief: Entrepreneurs respond to changing conditions with new ideas and technology, such as businesses that turn waste into products or sell clean energy.
